prompt.context: Our client, Vitality Insurance, is a leading provider of supplemental insurance products in the United States. Vitality agents partner with companies to offer their employees optional, supplemental insurance for such conditions as life, long-term disability, etc. Vitality has undergone fairly steady growth in the past two years, but profit margin is decreasing.
prompt.question: What should Vitality Insurance do about its declining profit margin?

clarifying_info.q: How large is Vitality and how does it sell?
clarifying_info.a: Vitality is the leader in its category with over 10,000 field sales agents (FSAs). All policies are sold through FSAs who are solely compensated on a percentage commission of total new premium (premium from new customers or additional premium up-sell from existing policyholders).

clarifying_info.q: Are there any other incentives beyond base commission?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. Short-term priorities are often communicated via sales contests that focus on a particular customer segment or activity and pay a bonus in addition to standard commission.

clarifying_info.q: What are the major cost categories?
What is the competitive environment like?
clarifying_info.a: There are few competitors in this mature market with similar growth. Vitality is a leader in the space; competition is not the primary focus.
Agent turnover is very high on a yearly basis, though it was lower during the recessionary period.

exhibits.title: Results and Costs
exhibits.shows: A table of Vitality Insurance key results and costs (figures in thousands) for 2008, 2009, and 2010, covering accounts converted, total policyholders enrolled, total premium from policyholders, and a breakdown of total costs into G&A, Sales, and Advertising, plus profit margin.

exhibits.title: Insurance Sales Process
exhibits.shows: A diagram of the insurance sales process showing leverage points (Hire new agents, Acquire new accounts, Keep accounts active, Upsell active accounts, Produce results / Premium $, Reactivating dormant account) and the number of sales contests targeted at each leverage point for 2008, 2009, and 2010.

exhibits.title: Snapshot of Sweeps Week Contest Results
exhibits.shows: A line chart comparing weekly premium ratios (ratio to average weekly premium 2008-2010) across weeks 1-27 (January-June) for 2008, 2009, and 2010, with two 2010 Sweeps Week periods marked (weeks 4 and 20).

data.y_axis: Ratio to Average Weekly Premium (2008-2010), ranging 0% to ~200%

framework: Understand the revenue and cost structure: decompose total premium growth vs. cost growth by line item
Identify which cost line is anomalous and quantify the deviation from trend
Investigate root causes of the sales cost spike: examine the sales compensation and incentive contest structure
Analyze whether new contest programs are aligned with or duplicative of the existing commission structure
Assess whether contests are driving incremental behavior or gaming/cannibalization of existing sales
Formulate recommendation to realign incentives and eliminate or repurpose misaligned programs

questions.prompt: Part 1: Look at Exhibit A and identify the key cost trends. What stands out?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note: (1) Accounts converted, policyholders enrolled, and premium all grow at ~10% per year consistently. (2) G&A and Advertising also grow at roughly 10% per year. (3) Sales costs grew 10% from 2008 to 2009 (in line with all other metrics) but then jumped 45% from 2009 to 2010, while premium growth remained 10%. (4) Profit margin declined meaningfully from 9.4% to 8.5% in 2010, pointing to the sales cost spike as the primary driver. Strong candidates will flag the anomaly quickly and calculate growth rates to confirm.

math.setup: Calculate year-over-year growth rates for each cost line and for revenue. Costs in $000s.
steps: Implied excess sales cost in 2010: if sales grew at 10% like premium, expected = 275 * 1.10 = $302.5k; actual = $400k; excess ~ $97.5k

Profit margin check 2010: Total costs = 58+400+30 = $488k; Revenue = $3,025,000k (note: revenue in absolute $, costs in $000s so costs = $488,000; margin = (3,025,000,000 - 488,000,000) / 3,025,000,000 is not directly computable from figures as given; use reported margin 8.5%)
math.answer: Sales costs grew 45% in 2010 vs. 10% revenue growth, accounting for the bulk of the margin compression from 9.4% to 8.5%.

questions.prompt: Part 2: Given the sales cost spike, what is the root cause? (Refer to Exhibit B and any additional information provided.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should: (1) Notice from Exhibit B that the contest mix shifted dramatically in 2010 — contests targeting 'Keep accounts active' dropped from 4 to 0, while contests targeting 'Acquire new accounts' and 'Produce results (Premium $)' each doubled from 2 to 4. (2) Recognize that the base commission already rewards 'total new premium,' so adding more contests on that same metric is duplicative and does not incentivize new behavior. (3) Absorb the additional detail about 'Sweeps Week': Vitality launched a contest paying an extra 10% bonus on all premium booked in two specific low-volume weeks. Agents liked it. (4) Connect the dots: the new premium-focused contests add bonus cost on top of commission for activity that would have occurred anyway.

questions.prompt: Part 3: Is Sweeps Week actually driving incremental premium, or is something else happening? (Refer to Exhibit C.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe from Exhibit C: (1) In Sweeps Week periods (weeks 4 and 20 in 2010), weekly premium spikes sharply — ratios reach ~150-200% of average. (2) However, the weeks immediately before and after each Sweeps Week show abnormally low premiums relative to 2008/2009 benchmarks. (3) This pattern implies agents are 'gaming' the system — pulling forward or pushing back sales into the Sweeps Week to earn the 10% bonus, rather than generating net new premium. (4) The net effect is little or no incremental premium but significant additional contest bonus cost paid out. Strong candidates will note agents have authority to influence enrollment timing by up to one week (if asked), which enables this behavior.

questions.prompt: Part 4 (Synthesis): Provide your final recommendation to Vitality Insurance.
questions.guidance: Strong recommendation covers: (1) Eliminate 'Sweeps Week' for 2011 — it is duplicative with the base commission (both target total premium), it enables gaming (agents shift timing rather than generate new volume), and it adds bonus cost with no net revenue benefit. (2) Repurpose those funds toward contest activities NOT already covered by the main commission structure — e.g., reactivating dormant accounts, or retaining existing policyholders, which are currently underincentivized (Keep accounts active contests dropped to zero in 2010). (3) Be cautious about the increase in new-account acquisition contests — acquiring new customers costs more than retaining existing ones, so this shift in contest mix is also likely hurting margins; consider rebalancing toward retention/upsell. (4) Acknowledge uncertainty: it is unclear whether the new-account focus reflects a deliberate strategic pivot; clarify with leadership before eliminating those contests.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond eliminating Sweeps Week, what other levers could Vitality use to improve or protect its profit margins?

categories.name: Revenue enhancement
ideas: Increase premium rates on existing policies
Expand into new supplemental product lines (dental, vision, critical illness)
Target higher-value employer segments
Improve upsell conversion on existing policyholders

categories.name: Sales force productivity
ideas: Redesign commission structure to reward retention and upsell, not just new premium
Introduce tiered commissions that reward higher-quality (longer-tenured) policy sales
Reduce agent turnover through better onboarding and career paths
Use data analytics to identify highest-performing agent behaviors and replicate them

categories.name: Contest / incentive redesign
ideas: Focus contests on behaviors not covered by base commission (reactivation, retention)
Cap contest bonuses to prevent gaming
Design contests with rolling measurement windows to prevent timing manipulation
Add clawback provisions if policies lapse shortly after booking

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Reduce G&A overhead through process automation
Renegotiate advertising spend or shift to lower-cost digital channels
Consolidate underperforming sales territories
Reduce cost of agent recruitment given high turnover

categories.name: Customer retention
ideas: Invest in policyholder communication and engagement programs
Offer loyalty discounts or coverage enhancements for long-tenure policyholders
Target employers with higher retention rates
Track and reduce lapse rates

recommendation: Eliminate the 'Sweeps Week' contest immediately for 2011, as it is duplicative with the base commission structure and incentivizes agents to game enrollment timing rather than generate incremental premium, driving up sales costs with no net revenue benefit.

Repurpose freed contest budget toward incentives targeting underserved stages of the sales process — particularly keeping accounts active and reactivating dormant accounts — to improve retention and reduce the higher cost of new customer acquisition.
risks: Agents may perceive the elimination of a popular contest negatively, potentially affecting morale or short-term productivity; change management and communication will be important.

The increase in new-account acquisition contests in 2010 may reflect a deliberate strategic growth initiative; eliminating or reducing it without clarity on strategic intent could conflict with company direction.
Redesigning incentive structures without careful modeling could create new unintended gaming behaviors.
next_steps: Confirm with Vitality leadership whether the shift to new-account acquisition in 2010 was a deliberate strategic choice or an unintended consequence of contest design.
Model the full-year cost impact of eliminating Sweeps Week and reallocating to retention-focused contests.
Audit other existing contests for similar duplication with the base commission structure.
Consider piloting a redesigned contest program in select regions before national rollout.
